## Result

Both tests agree: **all three years (1985, 1990, 1996) show a statistically significant wealth gap** in favour of the non-jailed group.

### Per-year table

| Year | U | z (MW) | p (MW) | r (rank-biserial) | t | df (Welch) | p (Welch) | Cohen's d | Descriptives (Mean₀ / Mean₁, Med₀ / Med₁) |
|------|---|--------|--------|-------------------|---|------------|-----------|-----------|---------------------------------------------|
| 1985 | 1 325 213 | −6.334 | 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ | 0.2178 | −5.244 | 303.6 | 2.9 × 10⁻⁷ | −0.3006 | 25 086 / 7 929, 3 600 / 720 |
| 1990 | 982 498 | −12.218 | 7.8 × 10⁻³⁵ | 0.4201 | −11.476 | 302.4 | 1.5 × 10⁻²⁵ | −0.6818 | 73 948 / 16 350, 10 500 / 0 |
| 1996 | 1 099 927 | −10.202 | 9.3 × 10⁻²⁶ | 0.3507 | −10.368 | 303.7 | 9.2 × 10⁻²² | −0.5917 | 105 447 / 20 383, 8 500 / 0 |

All p-values ≪ 0.05 in both tests. The jailed group (n = 289) has lower mean and median wealth in every year; the gap widens from 1985 → 1996 (rank-biserial r goes 0.22 → 0.42 → 0.35; Cohen's d goes −0.30 → −0.68 → −0.59 on the log scale).

### Hypothesis

> Individuals with a criminal record (ever_jailed = 1, i.e., incarcerated between 1985 and 1994) had significantly lower wealth than those without in 1985, 1990, and 1996. In every year tested, the jailed group's median and mean composite wealth were substantially lower (Mann-Whitney U test, two-sided, p < 0.05 in all three years; Welch t-test on log-transformed wealth confirmed the same pattern). Limitation: ever_jailed captures incarceration 1985–1994 only (not broader criminal history), and the raw two-group comparison does not adjust for race or sex confounding.

### No divergence between tests
Both the non-parametric and parametric tests identify the same three years as significant, so no controlled regression was needed.

payload.workflow: Loaded nls_incarceration_processed.csv (n=12013). Split by ever_jailed (0: n=11724, 1: n=289). For each of the three composite_wealth columns (1985, 1990, 1996), ran Mann-Whitney U (two-sided) as the primary test and Welch t-test on sign-preserving log1p-transformed wealth as the secondary test. alpha=0.05, no multiple-testing correction. Both tests agreed: all three years significant.
